I'm Ranjana. Last month at the team lunch, Gulnaz rolled her eyes about the new interns from the small-town colleges. 'Copy-paste machines. No brains, no English, just attendance.' People laughed. I almost did.
Instead I asked, 'Which one? Tell me about one of them.'
Gulnaz paused. 'Well... Mohit, the tall one.'
'What's Mohit like?'
'He comes in at eight because the bus from his village is the only one.' She stirred her dal. 'He asked me how to write a proper email. Twice.'
'Did he get it right the second time?'
She almost smiled. 'Better than some of us.'
The next week I saw her at Mohit's desk, going through his draft line by line. I think about that often. The whole group was easy to sneer at. One boy with a bus timetable wasn't.

qa.q: Why does Mohit come in at eight?
qa.a: Because the bus from his village is the only one.

qa.a: Talking about Mohit made her picture a real person who travels far and asked for help; she almost smiled, as if the sneer was harder to hold once she thought of him.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the lunch, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ranjana's question, 'Tell me about one of them', instead of laughing along; it moved Gulnaz from a sneer about a group to one person with a story.

qa.q: How might Mohit experience the change in Gulnaz the following week?
qa.a: Mohit now has a senior going through his draft line by line, which likely makes him feel noticed and helped rather than dismissed as a copy-paste machine.

Wednesday
At lunch Jatin was ranting because a parcel had gone missing. 'These delivery boys are all thieves. Animals on bikes. Can't trust any of them.' A couple of people nodded. I felt the old urge to just eat my rice and stay out of it. Instead I asked, 'What about Irfan? The one who comes every afternoon?' Jatin stopped. 'Irfan's okay.' 'He carried Mrs Joshi's water cans up four floors last month when the lift was broken. He's doing a correspondence degree; I've seen him reading on the stairs.' Jatin shrugged. 'Fine, Irfan's decent.' 'And the others you've never spoken to?' He didn't answer. After lunch he went down to ask Irfan about the parcel. It turned out to be sitting in reception with the wrong floor number on it.
Small thing. But I'm glad I didn't just eat my rice.
Ayesha

The café in Valencia was loud with the Saturday rush. Felix stirred his coffee hard.
“Those delivery riders are a plague. They all ride on the pavement. They're all the same, zero manners.”
Valentina nodded, then didn't. “All of them?”
“Every one.”
She glanced at the window. A rider in a green jacket was waiting by the pick-up shelf, rubbing his hands against the cold. She'd seen him before.
“That one,” she said. “Want to ask him something?” Before Felix could object, she held the door. “Hi, sorry. How many deliveries do you do on a Saturday?”
The rider blinked. “Thirty, if it goes well. My name's Joaquín. I'm saving for my engineering exams.” He smiled, tired. “Most people don't ask.”
When he left, Felix was quiet. “Okay. He's not a plague,” he admitted. “He's a guy who's cold.”

qa.q: How many deliveries does Joaquín do on a good Saturday?
qa.a: He does thirty deliveries on a Saturday if it goes well.

qa.q: Why did Valentina hesitate after first nodding?
qa.a: She felt uneasy with Felix's “all the same” contempt, because she had seen that rider before and knew he was one real person.

qa.q: What did Valentina do that worked?
qa.a: She turned a sweeping label into one conversation, asking the rider directly so Felix heard a name and a real story.

qa.q: How might Joaquín feel when a customer asks him a question?
qa.a: He might feel surprised and respected, since “most people don't ask,” and briefly less invisible.

grounding: The scene shows an adult responding to contempt for a group by talking to one person from it, which brings back empathy.

Dear Farida,

I have been meaning to write since Sunday.

You may not know this, but a few weeks ago, at the parish meeting, I heard someone call the families in the resettlement colony “encroachers,” people who “only take.” I nodded. I didn't know any of you.

Then on Sunday you told us about your brother Imran, who works double shifts at the bus depot and still teaches the colony children maths every evening under the streetlight. You told us how your mother cried when the demolition notice came.

I kept picturing Imran with the chalk and the streetlight. I couldn't nod again.

At the next meeting, I plan to ask whoever speaks that way which family they actually mean, and to invite you to speak if you're willing.

Thank you for telling me a real story.

Warmly,
Francis

Chaitanya, you said at lunch that the cleaning contractors are "all lazy". Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, new in this same office, and your Kavitha-ma'am was not much wiser.
Delivery riders used to wait in our lobby during the rains, and people complained. "They smell, they're rude, they're all the same." Something about "all the same" bothered me. So I asked Mr Rao, who complained loudest, "Which one? Tell me one name." He couldn't.
Next time it rained, I asked the rider by the door his name. Suresh. He was studying accounts at night college, and he waited inside because his phone had to stay dry for the orders. After that, "they" got harder for all of us to say.
So, Chaitanya. Which cleaner? What name?
